source.title: Unraveling the Mystery of Scaling Laws: Part I
source.authors: Hui Su; Zhi Tian; Xiaoyu Shen; Xun-Liang Cai

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present, including references; it is not an abstract-only or visibly cut-off excerpt.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains decoder-only Transformer language models, fits scaling relations for test cross-entropy loss, and checks predictions against larger runs using the same general loss-scaling measurement as the original work.
record.gate_note: The empirical fitted coefficients and actual-versus-predicted test-loss trajectories are recorded below. Citations to other studies' findings are not recorded as results. The paper also derives compute-allocation formulas and discusses uses for them, but does not empirically test whether the resulting fixed-compute allocation is optimal. It reports a general hyperparameter observation separately under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: Fits Kaplan-form power laws (L(N), L(N,Smin), Bcrit(L)) on 10 decoder-only Transformers of 1M–60M parameters for two datasets. It then checks predicted test-loss trajectories against 500M, 2B and 33B runs. This is the original measure (held-out cross-entropy) and the same functional forms.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that Kaplan's formula forms stay valid up to 33B, while the constants vary significantly with data, context length, tokenisation and model configuration. They say fits on 1M–60M models accurately predict minimum loss, required steps and tokens, critical batch size, and full loss trajectories for models up to 33B. They also derive, but do not test, compute-optimal N and S, and argue that models should not be trained to convergence.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the original power-law loss-scaling framework and held-out test-loss measure, while supplying a detailed estimation procedure and a finite-batch trajectory derivation. The experiments use C4 and a customized mixed-language dataset and predict runs up to 33B parameters.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper states that constants depend on context length, tokenization, data distribution, and model configurations. It reports that finite-batch loss-trajectory prediction depends on selecting an optimal learning rate; early warm-up stages can also reduce prediction accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Batch size, learning rate and learning-rate scheduler change convergence speed but not the final converged loss, within reasonable ranges and with ample non-repeated data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within reasonable ranges, optimisation hyperparameters change convergence rate, not converged loss.

fits_no_version.finding: A batch-size scan of a 10M model (Figure 2) is reported to verify (S/Smin−1)(E/Emin−1)=1, with critical-batch training costing 2x the minimum steps and tokens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The McCandlish step/token trade-off relation holds for LM pretraining.

record.problems: The paper provides no uncertainty estimates for fitted constants or prediction errors. Several prediction comparisons are available only as plots, and out-of-domain loss trajectories fluctuate substantially. The setup comparisons do not isolate every factor that may account for coefficient differences.
record.rows_left_out: No additional empirical prediction trajectories were reported in the text beyond those recorded. The paper's equations for optimal fixed-compute model size and training steps are not recorded as empirical test rows because the study does not experimentally evaluate those allocations.

untested.parts: Loss versus training-token count with other factors non-bottlenecked; loss versus compute; goodness of fit.
Quantitative prediction error; datasets beyond C4, the mixed set and private Chinese data; other architectures.
All of it. Optimal N(C) and S(C) are only derived analytically (Eq 5.1), not tested empirically.
All of it. The footnote that architectural bottlenecks destabilise estimation is not a fixed-N shape comparison.
All of it: other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer.
All of it; no downstream measures.
Bending away from a single power law; alternative fitting methods; parameter-counting or schedule effects on exponents; the compute-optimal split.

missing.what: The statement that trajectory prediction (Eq 3.13) is accurate only when the learning rate is optimally set; this is a dependence of V2 on a setup choice.
Figure 2 batch-size scan of a 10M model (4096 context) verifying Eq 3.11.
Training-token counts for the out-of-domain runs (500M/400B, 2B/1T, 33B/3T), which are missing from rows r9–r11.

record.verdict_notes: Rows r4–r6 are Kaplan et al. values (an original source) and should not count as this study's results. The comparison with Kaplan cannot support V7: C4 αN equals Kaplan's, and only the paper's own two setups contrast with each other. Those two setups also differ in several factors at once (data, context length, test set), so the cause of the coefficient differences is not isolated. No uncertainties or numeric prediction errors are given; all prediction evidence is figures plus text. Out-of-domain rows were upgraded from partial to observed because the fluctuations are in the actual loss and the authors report alignment; a reviewer may reasonably keep them as partial.

versions.untested_parts: The study fits loss relations to model size and training step, and critical-batch-size relations to loss. It does not independently sweep training-token count while holding the other variables non-bottlenecked, or validate the full claim across different architectures and setups.
Predictions are checked for the reported C4, mixed-language code, and private Chinese test settings, not across a broader range of models, datasets, or training setups.

The paper derives formulas for optimal model size and training steps at fixed compute, but does not empirically test the loss-minimising allocation or compare the growth rates of optimal parameter and token counts.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No experiments on other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.
No downstream-task performance measurements; the discussion only notes that evaluation criteria are often correlated with loss.

The paper reports setup-dependent fitted coefficients, but does not test whether curves bend away from a single power law or systematically compare alternative fitting methods and compute-optimal splits.
